analysis.one_liner: Bars for-profit corporations from running political action committees.
analysis.headline: The House never voted on the bill; it sat in the House Administration Committee until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend campaign finance law so that only nonprofit corporations could establish and operate a political action committee (PAC), the type of fund that lets a for-profit company collect voluntary contributions from its executives and employees and spend them on federal elections. Existing corporate PACs would have to shut down and disburse their balances within one year. The bill was introduced in October 2023 and referred to the House Administration Committee, which took no further action before the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters who want corporate money's direct pipeline into congressional campaigns reduced. Corporate PACs are a major source of campaign funding for sitting members of both parties, and banning them would force candidates to raise money from many small donors rather than from a few hundred corporate political funds.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits for-profit corporations from establishing or operating a separate segregated political fund (a corporate PAC), and requires existing corporate PACs to terminate and disburse their balances within one year of enactment.
Restricts the corporate PAC channel to tax-exempt nonprofit corporations, so companies can no longer use it to bundle employee contributions for federal candidates.
Removes corporate stockholders from the pool of people a PAC may solicit, leaving solicitation to executive and administrative personnel of the sponsoring nonprofit.

analysis.who_pays: For-profit corporations that operate PACs, and the members of Congress of both parties whose campaigns are funded in significant part by corporate PAC contributions.
analysis.who_pays_short: Corporations with PACs and their recipients

drawbacks.text: The bill leaves super PACs untouched. After the Supreme Court's Citizens United decision, corporations can spend unlimited money in elections through independent groups, so banning corporate PACs narrows one channel of corporate money while leaving a larger, less transparent one open.
The bill applies only to corporations and does not touch labor union PACs, which operate under parallel law; a critic can fairly call that an uneven restriction on organized political money.
Corporate PAC money is often the most disclosed and traceable form of corporate political spending; some reformers argue pushing it out would simply shift donors toward harder-to-track channels.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core change is real: it would shut down the corporate PAC structure that funnels bundled employee and executive money to sitting lawmakers, which government-reform groups have long targeted. But it is a narrow tool. Super PACs, lobbying, and trade-association spending would all remain, and union PACs would be untouched, so corporate influence over elections would shrink at the edges rather than be dismantled. Honest supporters would call this one piece of a larger reform, not a cure.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Administration Committee, which never took it up, so it died when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Josh Harder (D-CA) introduced the Ban Corporate PACs Act on October 12, 2023, joined by Jared Golden (D-ME).
The bill was referred to the House Committee on House Administration on October 25, 2023, and no further action appears in the record.
The Congress ended January 3, 2025, without the committee holding a markup or the House voting on the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Corporate PACs and the campaigns they fund, which keep an established fundraising channel because the bill never received a vote.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Corporate PACs and the members they fund

for.name: Josh Harder
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Ban Corporate PACs Act on October 12, 2023.

against.name: House Committee on House Administration
against.role: Committee of referral; controls whether election-law bills get a markup
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on October 25, 2023 and took no action on it for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Only two members of the House, both Democrats, put their names on the bill, and no roll-call vote was ever taken, so the parties' positions were never recorded.

industries.note: The bill would terminate roughly a thousand corporate PACs that bundle employee and executive money for federal candidates. Corporations would lose their most disclosed direct-contribution channel, though super PAC spending would remain available.

With corporate PACs shut down, donors seeking corporate influence would have an incentive to shift toward super PACs, which face no contribution limits and disclose less about their coordination with campaigns.

industries.industry: Political fundraising professionals and PAC consultants
industries.note: A one-year wind-down of existing corporate PACs would eliminate a large book of business for firms that operate and advise these funds.
